# Romans 12: research notes, verse by verse

**Gaps first.** I couldn't read anything for this chapter from the Methodist/Wesleyan, Pentecostal, Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox or modern-scholarship sites (wesley.nnu.edu, ag.org, lcms.org, newadvent.org, oca.org, netbible.org notes, bibleodyssey.org). I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of Romans 12. So those views are left out, except where an older commentator I did read mentions them. The Enduring Word and Ellicott pages cut off partway through, at v. 8 and v. 13. That's why vv. 14–19 have less material.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading.** Paul moves here from teaching to practical instruction for Christian living. His motive is a deep sense of God's mercy. Ellicott says "your bodies" means the body itself, the part of us most likely to lead us into sin. He reads "reasonable service" as service done *by* the reason, not service that reason *requires*. He also quotes Chrysostom: the eye that looks at no evil, the tongue that speaks nothing filthy and the hand that does no lawless deed each become an offering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/12.htm
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says we sacrifice ourselves because we already have God's favour, not to earn it. The mercies God describes in chapters 1-11 (justification, adoption, the Holy Spirit, assurance of glory) are what persuade our wills. He sees "body" as the whole person, and the picture as the burnt offering, where the whole animal was given to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-12/
- Matthew Henry: Christ is the only sacrifice of atonement; but our persons and performances, tendered to God through Christ our priest, are as sacrifices of acknowledgment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_012.cfm
- Pulpit Commentary: the Greek verb is the usual word for bringing an animal to the altar. "Reasonable service" refers to the act of offering, not the thing offered. It means moral, spiritual worship, as opposed to mechanical outward ritual. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/12.htm
- **Where traditions differ:**
  - *Grace and free will (Anglican, Pulpit Commentary).* The Pulpit Commentary reads Paul's appeals as showing that the fruit of faith will not grow unless the believer himself does his part in cultivating them. It says Paul holds that salvation is all of grace, and also the power of man's free-will to use or resist grace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/12.htm
  - *Reformed (Ligonier).* It's a living sacrifice because our Sacrifice lives and He brings life to us. Lord's Day worship together becomes the pattern for everyday personal worship. https://learn.ligonier.org/qas/what-does-it-mean-to-present-our-bodies-as-a-living-sacrifice-to-god
  - *Protestant vs. Catholic on the Mass.* Jamieson-Fausset-Brown use this verse against the Catholic teaching that the Mass is an "unbloody sacrifice" offered for sins. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Rom/Rom_012.cfm Got Questions says Protestants cite the verse to argue that Malachi's "pure offering" is fulfilled spiritually: believers can offer themselves as living sacrifices wherever they are. https://www.gotquestions.org/Holy-Eucharist.html (This is a Protestant site describing the Catholic view, not a Catholic source.)
  - *Churches of Christ (Coffman).* Coffman says the believer indeed presents his body for baptism, this being an important element in the new birth itself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/12-1.html

**v. 2**
- **Traditional reading.** Ellicott: the two verbs differ. One means outward conformity, a kind of disguise. The other means a thorough change from within. "This world" means the present age, set against the Messiah's new reign. "Prove" means first to discern God's will and then to choose and do it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/12.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: "schema" (fashion) is outward and passing, while "morphe" (form) is essential. The verbs are in the present tense, which points to ongoing habits. In its words, the perfect Christian character "is not formed all at once on conversion." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/12.htm
- Guzik: the battle happens in the mind. A life built only on feelings, or only on doing, misses the transformation. The Greek *metamorphoo* is the same word used of Jesus' transfiguration. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-12/
- Pulpit Homiletics: We cannot renew our own minds. "Except a man be born from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/romans/12.htm

**v. 3**
- **Traditional reading.** Ellicott: "the grace given me" means Paul's apostolic authority. There is a Greek wordplay, roughly "not to be high-minded beyond what one ought, but minded toward sober-mindedness." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/12.htm
- **"Measure of faith": readings differ.**
  - Ellicott: faith comes in different amounts. Those with the strongest faith may take on the highest roles, provided they judge themselves honestly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/12.htm
  - Pulpit Commentary: Paul says "faith" rather than "grace" because faith is how we receive grace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/12.htm
  - Guzik: even our saving faith is God's gift, so we have no grounds for pride. Spiritual giftedness is not the same as spiritual maturity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-12/

**vv. 4–5**
- Ellicott: Christ unites the church the way a person's will unites the body. "Members one of another" really means fellow-members. He also sees in the picture a division of labour, even a hierarchy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/12.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: unlike Ephesians, these verses do not single out Christ as the Head. The whole is "one body in Christ." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/12.htm
- Guzik: the church has unity but not uniformity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-12/

**v. 6: "in proportion to his faith" (a real disagreement)**
- *Objective, "the rule of faith" (Calvin, Reformed).* Prophets must conform their prophecies to the rule of faith, lest in anything they should deviate from the right line. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/12-6.html
- *Gill (Baptist).* These gifts are ordinary, not extraordinary, and will last until the end of time. "Prophesying" here means preaching the Gospel, not foretelling. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/12-6.html
- *Matthew Henry (both readings).* It means preaching, measured by how much faith the preacher has, and also according to the proportion of the doctrine of faith, as it is revealed in the holy scriptures. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/12-6.html
- *Subjective, the prophet's own faith (Ellicott, Pulpit, Barnes).* Ellicott: what the prophet says should not outrun the faith he is aware of in himself. Otherwise preaching becomes "rhetorical and insincere." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/12.htm The Pulpit Commentary rejects the "analogy of faith" reading outright. It says that reading is not in the Greek Fathers and was apparently first suggested by Thomas Aquinas. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/12.htm Barnes: It means the measure, the amount of faith bestowed on them. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/romans/12-6.html
- *Guzik (Enduring Word, listed with the Pentecostal/charismatic sites).* Prophecy is mainly "forth-telling" God's heart. If you can't prophesy in faith, trusting God has really spoken, don't do it. He warns against casual "Thus says the Lord." He also notes the Greek has "*the* faith," which may point to agreement with accepted doctrine. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-12/
- *Translations.* Wesley's own New Testament renders it according to the analogy of faith. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wes/romans/12-6.html The Catholic Douay-Rheims has to be used according to the rule of faith. https://biblehub.com/parallel/romans/12-6.htm

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: "ministry" is the technical term for the deacon's office (Acts 6). It covered practical work such as giving out alms and caring for the poor and sick. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/12.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary disagrees: the word should be taken generally, not only of deacons. These are gifts of all Christians, not distinct church offices. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/12.htm
- Guzik: teaching instructs, and exhortation urges people to live out what they've been taught. Both are needed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-12/

**v. 8**
- *Church offices or every believer?* Gill (Baptist) reads the giving, leading and mercy as branches of the deacon's office. "Giving" means handing out the church's money to proper objects, honestly and impartially. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/12-8.htm Ellicott says that from "he that giveth" onward Paul turns to duties common to all members. "Simplicity" means a single motive, with no thought of self-exaltation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/12.htm
- Ellicott on mercy with cheerfulness: The kindness of charity is doubled when it is done in a cheerful and kindly way. Cheerfulness is a duty to cultivate, not just a matter of temperament. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/12.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: givers should give "in simplicity," which may mean singleness of heart, without partiality or show. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/12.htm

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: the Greek word means "without hypocrisy." Love should come from real feeling, built on a strong hatred of evil and an equally strong hold on good. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/12.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: "kindly affectioned" is a word for family love, which suits the Christian family. "Preferring" may mean taking the lead: show honour first, without waiting to receive it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/12.htm

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: the KJV's "business" really means zeal. The verse is about the spiritual life, not daily work. "Fervent" literally means boiling. "In spirit" means the believer's own spirit, not the Holy Spirit. Some ancient copies read "serving the time," which he thinks is wrong. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/12.htm
- Another commentator on the Bible Hub page says the thought "you are serving the Lord" should revive us when we start to droop and grow cold. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/12-11.htm

**v. 12**
- Ellicott links the hope here to Romans 8:20–25. Patience in trouble was especially needed in those hard times for the church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/12.htm
- Another commentator on the Bible Hub page: patience in trouble depends on joyful hope, and hope is strengthened by prayer, so all depends on our "perseverance in prayer." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/12-12.htm

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: "saints" simply means Christians. The hospitality in view was more than entertaining friends. Persecuted believers were often driven from city to city and needed shelter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/12.htm
- Another commentator on the Bible Hub page: "given to hospitality" literally means *pursuing* hospitality. Barnes adds that the duty still applies even though inns now exist. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/12-13.htm

**v. 14**
- Pulpit Commentary: here Paul switches from participles to direct commands because a positive command of Christ being adduced. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/12-12.htm
- Piper: the goal in loving enemies is v. 14, bless and do not curse, as in Paul's prayer for Israel's salvation (Romans 10:1). https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/christ-overcame-evil-with-good-do-the-same

**v. 15**
- I didn't find any commentary on this verse in the pages I read.

**v. 16**
- Matthew Henry, on "be not wise in your own conceits": It is good to be wise, but it is bad to think ourselves so. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/12-20.html

**vv. 17–18**
- Pulpit Commentary: peace with everyone may sometimes be impossible, but at any rate, do not increase bitterness by avenging yourselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/12.htm

**v. 19**
- Pulpit Commentary: this verse follows naturally from v. 18. The quotation appears in the same form in Hebrews 10:30, which suggests it was a saying in common use. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/12.htm

**v. 20: "burning coals" (a real disagreement)**
- *Shame, remorse and repentance (the majority view).*
  - Gill (Baptist) rejects the idea that kindness is meant to increase God's wrath on the enemy. Instead the enemy's conscience is stung and he is led to repent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/12-20.htm
  - Expositor's Greek Testament: it must refer to the burning pain of shame and remorse which the man feels whose hostility is repaid by love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/12-20.htm
  - Barclay, Smith and Barnes read it the same way. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/12-20.html
- *Melting metal.* Adam Clarke (Methodist) thinks the picture probably comes from smelting metals and that it means a good effect. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/12-20.html Matthew Henry: kindness melts the enemy into repentance and friendship, as David's mercy melted Saul. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/12-20.html
- *God's judgment if the enemy refuses.* Constable prefers this view because in the Old Testament "coals of fire" consistently mean God's anger. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/12-20.html
  - Piper (Baptist, Desiring God) says he knows of no evidence that coals on the head stand for blessing. He thinks the phrase most naturally refers to justice: the more mercy they reject, the more coals of fire will be heaped on their head. This is not our desire or our aim. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/christ-overcame-evil-with-good-do-the-same
  - Calvin mentions that some take the coals to mean destruction coming back on the enemy, because his guilt is doubled. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/12-20.html
  - Poole leaves both options open: the enemy will either relent or bring greater vengeance from God on himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/12-20.htm
- *The custom of carrying a pot of coals.* Some explain the verse by a custom of giving a neighbour a pot of live coals, carried on the head, to restart his fire. This makes the coals an act of generosity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/12-20.html Piper says he has heard of this custom but is not persuaded by it. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/christ-overcame-evil-with-good-do-the-same
- *Got Questions* reads v. 21 as explaining v. 20. The coals most likely mean burning shame, though coals also stand for judgment and purification elsewhere in the Bible. https://www.gotquestions.org/burning-coals.html

**v. 21**
- Barclay: To stoop to vengeance is to be ourselves conquered by evil. Evil can never be conquered by evil. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/12-20.html
- Piper grounds vv. 20–21 in Holy Week: Christ died for his enemies. Even if loving an enemy seems to fail and costs your life, you have still overcome evil, and you will be vindicated at the resurrection. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/christ-overcame-evil-with-good-do-the-same
